translationRepairs: As the court prepared to install their spirit tablets in the Imperial Ancestral Temple and rank Emperor Gaozu as a collateral forebear, the Grand Marshal and acting Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Prince Huai of Linhuai, Yuan Yu, submitted a memorial of protest: "Emperor Gaozu of Han raised a temple to the Supreme Emperor on Fragrant Street, and Emperor Guangwu worshipped his father at Chunling.

As the court prepared to install their spirit tablets in the Imperial Ancestral Temple and rank Emperor Gaozu as a collateral forebear, the Grand Marshal and acting Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Prince of Linhuai, Yuan Yu, submitted a memorial of protest: "Emperor Gaozu of Han raised a temple to the Supreme Emperor on Fragrant Street, and Emperor Guangwu worshipped his father at Chunling.
臨淮王彧 is the Prince of Linhuai named Yu; Huai is part of the fief 臨淮, not a second princely name stacked on Linhuai.

When they were about to move the spirit tablets to the Imperial Ancestral Temple and treat Emperor Gaozu as an uncle in the patriline, the Grand Marshal and Acting Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Prince Huai of Linhuai, Yuan Yu, memorialized in protest, saying: "Emperor Gaozu of Han established the temple of the Supreme Emperor at Xiang Street, and Emperor Guangwu enshrined his father at Chunling.

When they were about to move the spirit tablets to the Imperial Ancestral Temple and treat Emperor Gaozu as an uncle in the patriline, the Grand Marshal and Acting Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Prince of Linhuai, Yuan Yu, memorialized in protest, saying: "Emperor Gaozu of Han established the temple of the Supreme Emperor at Xiang Street, and Emperor Guangwu enshrined his father at Chunling.
The literal likewise misreads 臨淮王 as Prince Huai of Linhuai; Prince of Linhuai matches the title.
On renyin, Wei ordered Prince Ye of Jiyin to serve concurrently as acting Director of the Imperial Secretariat on the mobile staff and to place Qiu Daqian and others in command of the Liang region.

On renyin, Wei ordered Prince Huiye of Jiyin to serve concurrently as acting Director of the Imperial Secretariat on the mobile staff and to place Qiu Daqian and others in command of the Liang region.
暉業 is Huiye; Ye keeps only the last syllable and invents a different personal name.
On day renyin, Wei ordered Prince Ye of Jiyin to act as Director of the Imperial Secretariat on the mobile staff and to command Qiu Daqian and others in garrisoning the Liang region.
On day renyin, Wei ordered Prince Huiye of Jiyin to act as Director of the Imperial Secretariat on the mobile staff and to command Qiu Daqian and others in garrisoning the Liang region.
The literal Prince Ye truncates 暉業; Huiye is the name in the Chinese.
Ye was a great-grandson of the Lesser Xin Prince Cheng.
Huiye was a great-grandson of Xiao Xincheng.
暉業 is Huiye, and 小新成 is the three-character name Xiao Xincheng, not a title 'Lesser Xin Prince Cheng'.
Ye was a great-grandson of the Lesser Xin Prince Cheng.
Huiye was a great-grandson of Xiao Xincheng.
The same two names are wrong in the literal: Huiye and Xiao Xincheng restore 暉業 and 小新成.
In the third month, on renxu, Wei ordered the Prince of Shangdang, Yuan Tianmu, to suppress Xing Luo, appointing Fei Mu grand commander of the vanguard.
In the third month, on renxu, Wei ordered the Prince of Shangdang, Yuan Tianmu, to suppress Xing Gao, appointing Fei Mu grand commander of the vanguard.
邢杲 is Xing Gao; Luo would be 羅 or a misreading of 杲, not this graph.
In the third month, on day renxu, Wei ordered the Prince of Shangdang, Yuan Tianmu, to campaign against Xing Luo, with Fei Mu as Grand Commander of the Vanguard.
In the third month, on day renxu, Wei ordered the Prince of Shangdang, Yuan Tianmu, to campaign against Xing Gao, with Fei Mu as Grand Commander of the Vanguard.
The literal Xing Luo does not match 邢杲; Gao is the correct reading of 杲.
Prince Huai of Linhuai, Yuan Yu, remonstrated: "Nothing like this exists in antiquity. Your Majesty acts without precedent—what will later ages make of it!"
Prince of Linhuai, Yuan Yu, remonstrated: "Nothing like this exists in antiquity. Your Majesty acts without precedent—what will later ages make of it!"
臨淮王 is Prince of Linhuai; Huai is not a posthumous name separate from the fief.
Prince Huai of Linhuai, Yuan Yu, remonstrated, saying: "Such a thing has never existed in antiquity. Your Majesty acts without precedent—what will posterity think!"
Prince of Linhuai, Yuan Yu, remonstrated, saying: "Such a thing has never existed in antiquity. Your Majesty acts without precedent—what will posterity think!"
The literal Prince Huai of Linhuai doubles 淮; Prince of Linhuai is the title in the Chinese.

Yuan Tianmu of Wei was preparing to attack Xing Luo when word came that the Prince of Beihai, Yuan Hao, was raiding the borders; he convened civil and military officers for counsel, and all said, "Luo's forces are strong—we should strike him first."

Yuan Tianmu of Wei was preparing to attack Xing Gao when word came that the Prince of Beihai, Yuan Hao, was raiding the borders; he convened civil and military officers for counsel, and all said, "Gao's forces are strong—we should strike him first."
邢杲 and the later 杲 name Xing Gao, not Luo, including in the quoted 杲眾強盛.

Yuan Tianmu of Wei was about to strike Xing Luo when the Prince of Beihai, Yuan Hao, was invading; he gathered civil and military officials to deliberate, and all said: "Luo's host is strong and should be dealt with first."

Yuan Tianmu of Wei was about to strike Xing Gao when the Prince of Beihai, Yuan Hao, was invading; he gathered civil and military officials to deliberate, and all said: "Gao's host is strong and should be dealt with first."
Both 邢杲 and 杲眾 must be Gao, not Luo.
The mobile-staff Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Xue Zan, said, "Xing Luo may field many men, but they are mere thieves and scavengers without distant ambition.
The mobile-staff Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Xue Shu, said, "Xing Gao may field many men, but they are mere thieves and scavengers without distant ambition.
薛琡 is Xue Shu (琡, not 瓚/Zan), and 邢杲 is Xing Gao.
The Director of the Imperial Secretariat on the mobile staff, Xue Zan, said: "Though Xing Luo's troops are many, they are rats stealing and dogs snatching, without far-reaching aims.
The Director of the Imperial Secretariat on the mobile staff, Xue Shu, said: "Though Xing Gao's troops are many, they are rats stealing and dogs snatching, without far-reaching aims.
The literal Xue Zan / Xing Luo pair mismatches 薛琡 and 邢杲.
Tianmu, since most commanders wanted to hit Luo and the Wei court likewise judged Hao isolated and negligible, ordered his forces first to pacify Qi and only then turn on Hao; he marched east.
Tianmu, since most commanders wanted to hit Gao and the Wei court likewise judged Hao isolated and negligible, ordered his forces first to pacify Qi and only then turn on Hao; he marched east.
擊杲 refers to Xing Gao; Luo is not in the Chinese.

Tianmu, because most generals wished to strike Luo and the Wei court also regarded Hao as isolated and not worth worry, ordered Tianmu and the others first to settle Qi territory and then return to attack Hao; he led his army east.

Tianmu, because most generals wished to strike Gao and the Wei court also regarded Hao as isolated and not worth worry, ordered Tianmu and the others first to settle Qi territory and then return to attack Hao; he led his army east.
The same 杲 in the literal must be Gao, not Luo.
Prince Ye of Jiyin led twenty thousand armored guards at Kao city; Qingzhi stormed the place, took the city, and captured Ye.
Prince Huiye of Jiyin led twenty thousand armored guards at Kao city; Qingzhi stormed the place, took the city, and captured Huiye.
濟陰王暉業 and 擒暉業 name Huiye throughout; Ye truncates the personal name.
Prince Ye of Jiyin led twenty thousand armored guards at Kao city; Qingzhi stormed the city, captured it, and seized Ye.
Prince Huiye of Jiyin led twenty thousand armored guards at Kao city; Qingzhi stormed the city, captured it, and seized Huiye.
The literal likewise must keep Huiye for both 暉業 in this unit.
On xinchou, the Wei Prince of Shangdang, Yuan Tianmu, and Erzhu Zhao routed Xing Luo at Ji'nan; Luo surrendered, was sent to Luoyang, and beheaded.
On xinchou, the Wei Prince of Shangdang, Yuan Tianmu, and Erzhu Zhao routed Xing Gao at Ji'nan; Gao surrendered, was sent to Luoyang, and beheaded.
破邢杲 and 杲降 name Xing Gao, who then surrenders and is beheaded.
On day xinchou, the Prince of Shangdang, Yuan Tianmu, and Erzhu Zhao of Wei defeated Xing Luo at Ji'nan; Luo surrendered, was sent to Luoyang, and executed.
On day xinchou, the Prince of Shangdang, Yuan Tianmu, and Erzhu Zhao of Wei defeated Xing Gao at Ji'nan; Gao surrendered, was sent to Luoyang, and executed.
The literal Xing Luo / Luo does not transcribe 邢杲 / 杲.
Prince Huai of Linhuai, Yuan Yu, and Prince of Anfeng, Yuan Yanming, led the hundred officials to seal the treasuries and prepared the imperial equipage to welcome Hao.
The Prince of Linhuai, Yuan Yu, and the Prince of Anfeng, Yuan Yanming, led the hundred officials to seal the treasuries and prepared the imperial equipage to welcome Hao.
臨淮王彧 is the Prince of Linhuai, Yu; Huai is not a stacked princely name, and 安豐王延明 is a separate title.
Prince Huai of Linhuai, Yuan Yu, and Prince of Anfeng, Yuan Yanming, led the hundred officials to seal the treasuries and storehouses and prepared the imperial equipage to welcome Hao.
The Prince of Linhuai, Yuan Yu, and the Prince of Anfeng, Yuan Yanming, led the hundred officials to seal the treasuries and storehouses and prepared the imperial equipage to welcome Hao.
The literal Prince Huai of Linhuai makes the same inversion of 臨淮王.
Yang Chun remained in Luoyang; his younger brother Shun was inspector of Ji, and his nephew Kan was Northern Palace General—all were with the Wei emperor in Hebei.
Yang Chun remained in Luoyang; his younger brother Shun was inspector of Ji, and his nephew Kan was Northern Palace General, following the Wei emperor in Hebei.
楊椿在洛陽 is opposed to 從魏主在河北, which cannot include Chun; dropping 'all were' restores that split.
Yang Chun was in Luoyang; Chun's younger brother Shun was regional inspector of Ji, and his nephew Kan was Northern Palace General—all followed the Wei ruler in Hebei.
Yang Chun was in Luoyang; Chun's younger brother Shun was regional inspector of Ji, and his nephew Kan was Northern Palace General, following the Wei ruler in Hebei.
The literal 'all followed' likewise puts Chun, who is in Luoyang, into the Hebei suite.
The Wei emperor was about to flee before Hao and did not know where to turn; some urged Chang'an. The Palace Attendant Gao Daomu said, "Guanzhong lies in ruins—how can we go back there!
The Wei emperor was about to flee before Hao and did not know where to turn; some urged Chang'an. The Secretariat Drafter Gao Daomu said, "Guanzhong lies in ruins—how can we go back there!
中書舍人 is Secretariat Drafter, not the palace office 侍中.
The Wei ruler was about to leave to avoid Hao and did not know where to go; some urged Chang'an. The Palace Attendant Gao Daomu said: "Guanzhong is wasted and ruined—how can we go there again!
The Wei ruler was about to leave to avoid Hao and did not know where to go; some urged Chang'an. The Secretariat Drafter Gao Daomu said: "Guanzhong is wasted and ruined—how can we go there again!
The literal Palace Attendant is the same wrong office for 中書舍人.
Zisheng said, "Because tiger pass was lost, affairs came to this pass.
Zisheng said, "His Majesty, because Hulao was lost, has come to this pass.

主上 is the Wei sovereign and 虎牢 is Hulao, so 'tiger pass' is wrong; but 以虎牢失守 is the fall of Hulao, not that His Majesty himself lost the fortress, and 致此狼狽 has the sovereign as the one in the predicament.
Zisheng said: "Because Your Lordship lost Hulao, things came to this pass.
Zisheng said: "His Majesty, because Hulao was lost, has come to this pass.
主上 is not Tianmu as 'Your Lordship'; the proposed 'His Majesty lost Hulao' still makes the emperor the agent of 失守, whereas 虎牢失守 is the fortress falling and 主上 is the subject of 致此狼狽.
Qingzhi pressed on to Hulao; Erzhu Shilong abandoned the city and fled, and they took the Wei Eastern Palace Attendant, Xin Zuan.
Qingzhi pressed on to Hulao; Erzhu Shilong abandoned the city and fled, and they took the Wei Eastern Gentleman-General, Xin Zuan.
東中郎將 is an eastern gentleman-general command, not 侍中 / Palace Attendant.
Qingzhi pressed the attack on Hulao; Erzhu Shilong abandoned the city and fled, and they captured the Wei Eastern Palace Attendant Xin Zuan.
Qingzhi pressed the attack on Hulao; Erzhu Shilong abandoned the city and fled, and they captured the Wei Eastern Gentleman-General Xin Zuan.
The literal Eastern Palace Attendant is the same misreading of 東中郎將.

Or, if victory and defeat are hard to foresee, then it is better to take carriage and guest and cross the river, summon the Grand General Tianmu and the Grand Chancellor Rong each to bring troops to join, and advance in pincers—within ten days or a month success will appear.

Or, if victory and defeat are hard to foresee, then it is better to take the imperial carriage and cross the river, summon the Grand General Tianmu and the Grand Chancellor Rong each to bring troops to join, and advance in pincers—within ten days or a month success will appear.
CText reads 車駕, not 車賀; 'carriage and guest' treats 賀 as guest, while 車駕 is the imperial carriage.
Prince Jingxian of Pingyang, Jingxian, raised troops at He Bridge to attack Hao, failed, and died.
Prince Jingxian of Pingyang raised troops at He Bridge to attack Hao, failed, and died.
平陽王敬先 names the prince once; repeating Jingxian after the title has no Chinese counterpart.

Wei appointed Palace Attendant, Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat Erzhu Shilong bearer of the staff, acting mobile-staff vice director, grand general, and inspector of Xiang, to hold Ye city.

Wei appointed Palace Attendant, Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat Erzhu Shilong bearer of the staff, acting mobile-staff vice director, grand general, and inspector of Xiangzhou, to hold Ye city.
相州刺史 with seat at 鄴城 is Xiangzhou, not the same 襄州 collapsed as Xiang.
Once the Prince of Beihai, Yuan Hao, had achieved his aim, he secretly plotted to turn against Liang with Princes Huai of Linhuai and Anfeng, Yuan Yu and Yuan Yanming;
Once the Prince of Beihai, Yuan Hao, had achieved his aim, he secretly plotted to turn against Liang with the Prince of Linhuai, Yuan Yu, and the Prince of Anfeng, Yuan Yanming;
The fused 'Princes Huai of Linhuai and Anfeng' is a real error, but the proposed line still calls 臨淮王 'Prince Huai of Linhuai'; 臨淮王彧 and 安豐王延明 are two distinct fief titles, with Huai only in Linhuai.

The southern troops in Luo numbered fewer than ten thousand, while the Qiang and Hu were ten times as many; the army aide Ma Fonian spoke for Qingzhi: "General, your prestige runs through He and Luo and your name shakes the central plain; your merit is high and your power heavy—the Wei court will suspect you; once unforeseen change arises, can you be without worry!

The southern troops in Luo numbered fewer than ten thousand, while the Qiang and Hu were ten times as many; the army aide Ma Fonian said to Qingzhi: "General, your prestige runs through He and Luo and your name shakes the central plain; your merit is high and your power heavy—the Wei court will suspect you; once unforeseen change arises, can you be without worry!
為慶之曰 introduces speech addressed to Qingzhi, not speech on his behalf.
The General Who Subdues Waves, Yang Xin the Corrector of Ping, lived with his clan at Horse Ford and offered several small boats as guide.
The General Who Subdues Waves, Yang Xin of Zhengping, lived with his clan at Horse Ford and offered several small boats as guide.
正平 is the commandery Zhengping attached to 楊心剽, not an office 'Corrector of Ping'.
The General Who Subdues Waves, Yang Xin the Corrector of Ping, lived with his clan at Ma islet and said he had several small boats, asking to serve as guide.
The General Who Subdues Waves, Yang Xin of Zhengping, lived with his clan at Ma islet and said he had several small boats, asking to serve as guide.
The literal 'Corrector of Ping' invents an office from the place-name 正平.
On day renshen, the Grand Chancellor Rong was further ennobled as Grand General of the Heavenly Pillar, with fief increased by two hundred thousand households including previous grants.
On day renshen, the Grand Chancellor Rong was further made Grand General of the Heavenly Pillar, with fief increased by two hundred thousand households including previous grants.
加…天柱大將軍 adds a generalship; 增封 is the separate fief increase, so 'ennobled as' misstates 加.
Prince Huai of Linhuai, Yuan Yu, submitted again to the Wei emperor; Prince of Anfeng, Yuan Yanming, fled in with wife and children.
The Prince of Linhuai, Yuan Yu, submitted again to the Wei emperor; the Prince of Anfeng, Yuan Yanming, fled in with wife and children.
臨淮王彧 is the Prince of Linhuai, Yu; Huai is not a posthumous name split from the fief.
On jiaxu, Wei made the Prince of Shangdang, Yuan Tianmu, Grand Preceptor, and the Prince of Chengyang, Hui, Grand Marshal and Grand Commandant.
On jiaxu, Wei made the Prince of Shangdang, Yuan Tianmu, Grand Preceptor, and the Prince of Chengyang, Hui, Grand Marshal and concurrent Grand Commandant.
兼太尉 marks the Grand Commandant post as concurrent with 大司馬, which 'and' conceals.
In the eighth month, on jiwei, Wei made Grand Tutor Li Yanbao Minister of Education.
In the eighth month, on jiwei, Wei made Grand Tutor Li Yanshi Minister of Education.
李延寔 is Yanshi (寔); Yanbao would require 寶 and is not in the Chinese.
On day guimao, the hundred officials with one hundred million cash prayed to the white Three Jewels to ransom the Emperor Bodhisattva; the monastic assembly silently assented.
On day guimao, the hundred officials with one hundred million cash prayed and announced to the Three Jewels to ransom the Emperor Bodhisattva; the monastic assembly silently assented.
祈白三寶 is to pray and announce to the Three Jewels; 白 is the verb, not the color white.
Erzhu Rong sent Grand Commander Marquis Yuan of Jianshan to campaign against Han Lou at Ji with very few men—only seven hundred horsemen.
